workloads.consumer: inference request, model-load or rendering-frame helper owner
workloads.task: Discover 32 Status-bearing helper tasks while processing one owner, stop admission, retain the first business failure, drain every helper and complete runtime cleanup before owner return.
workloads.lifecycle: The paired direct-source process creates one persistent four-worker Scheduler, executes 4096 measurement-excluded owners per route in alternating order, then nanobench compare measures complete owners with one common iteration count over 52 paired interleaved rounds (cyclic Latin-square order; ABBA or BAAB for two routes). Each owner creates all helper coroutine frames, admits them dynamically, lets every helper yield once, validates every output, aggregates one failure in roughly one of sixteen owners, crosses Scheduler::drain after result visibility and tears down all ownership before the next owner.
workloads.semantic_equivalence: The candidate uses TaskScope::add and the peer composes public SpinLock, CancelToken, spawn_task, a same-allocator PMR handle vector, every-handle join and first-error retention. Both use the same normal persistent Scheduler and allocator, receive the same alternating 4096-owner warmup and run with one common calibrated iteration count in interleaved paired rounds, so frequency, thermal, stack-pool and allocator drift are shared rather than assigned to one entire route. Both call the public Scheduler::drain fence after result visibility, so Fiber finish hooks, coroutine/driver cleanup and stack return are charged before owner return. Both then destroy their retained owner records before returning.
workloads.negative_space: This is not detached fire-and-forget, a fixed compile-time when_all pack, a bare WaitGroup counter, an admission-unaware handle vector, a worker-stack callback or an IO/backend latency benchmark. A result-visible-only boundary is explicitly excluded because it lets the manual peer defer runtime cleanup. Separate product processes are also excluded: the primary consumer links both public routes from the same HYLE source graph, and a cross-process pair introduced a first-process bias absent from that journey.
